Warp
WAWRP
noun
From the Saxon wearp, from weorpan, “to throw or cast” — the threads cast lengthwise upon the loom and stretched taut between the beams before ever a shuttle crosses them.

Biblical Definition

The warp is the lengthwise thread of the loom: the set of strands strung upon the beams, held in tension, and fixed in place before the weaving begins. It is not the pattern that the eye admires; it is the skeleton the pattern hangs upon. Take the warp away and there is no cloth, only a heap of yarn. Scripture uses the word almost wholly in one place, and that place is a chapter about defilement. In the law of the leprosy of garments the priest is charged to examine not merely the surface of the cloth but its structure: “Whether it be in the warp, or woof; of linen, or of woollen; whether in a skin, or in any thing made of skin” (Lev 13:48). The plague is traced into the very threads. If it has entered the warp, no scouring of the face of the garment will do; the whole must be burnt (Lev 13:52). That is the doctrine the loom is made to teach. Sin in Scripture is never a stain lying upon an otherwise sound nature; it has gone down into the lengthwise threads of the man, into the frame upon which every thought and word and work is woven. Total depravity is warp-depravity. And this is why the remedy is not laundering but a new creation — not a garment washed, but a garment given, the imputed righteousness of Christ, woven whole from above.

Webster 1828 Definition

The threads extended lengthwise in the loom, crossed by the woof; hence the foundation-threads of any woven cloth.

expand to see more

WARP, n. [Sax. wearp, from weorpan, to cast or throw.] In manufactures, the threads which are extended lengthwise in the loom, and crossed by the woof.

To warp, in the verbal sense, is to turn or twist out of shape by unequal shrinking — whence the figurative use for a mind turned aside from rectitude.

The warp is strung and stretched before weaving begins; the woof is thrown across it by the shuttle.

Scripture employs the term in the law of leprosy in garments, distinguishing the plague in the warp from the plague in the woof (Lev 13:48-59).

Figuratively, the ground-work or substance of any thing; that upon which the rest is wrought.

Key Scripture

Lev 13:48 — "Whether it be in the warp, or woof; of linen, or of woollen; whether in a skin, or in any thing made of skin;"

Lev 13:49 — "And if the plague be greenish or reddish in the garment, or in the skin, either in the warp, or in the woof, or in any thing of skin; it is a plague of leprosy, and shall be shewed unto the priest:"

Lev 13:52 — "He shall therefore burn that garment, whether warp or woof, in woollen or in linen, or any thing of skin, wherein the plague is: for it is a fretting leprosy; it shall be burnt in the fire."

Lev 13:59 — "This is the law of the plague of leprosy in a garment of woollen or linen, either in the warp, or woof, or any thing of skins, to pronounce it clean, or to pronounce it unclean."

Modern Corruption

The garment law of Lev 13 is emptied of doctrine and re-labelled an ancient sanitation code — mildew management for a pre-scientific people — which silences everything the warp was meant to preach.

expand to see more

The common modern handling of Lev 13 is to reduce it to public health: a bronze-age quarantine manual for mould in cloth, interesting to the antiquarian, binding on no one, teaching nothing. The reduction is tidy and it is false, and the text itself refutes it. A sanitation officer does not need a priest; this examination is committed to the priest, at the door of the tabernacle, and its verdict is not safe or unsafe but clean or unclean — a standing before God, not a hazard to the lungs. A sanitation code does not require a garment to be brought out and burnt when a washing would serve, nor does it call the spot a fretting leprosy, borrowing the vocabulary of the plague in human flesh from the chapter’s first half. The law is deliberately teaching by analogy: what leprosy is in the body, this is in the cloth, and both are parables of what sin is in the sinner. Strip the doctrine out and you keep the hygiene and lose the gospel, which is precisely the trade the rationalist reading proposes.

Recover the lesson the warp was strung to teach. First, that sin penetrates: it does not sit on the surface of a nature otherwise sound but runs in the lengthwise threads, so that the whole man — mind, will, affections — is implicated. Second, that God’s inspection is total. The priest looks past the face of the cloth into its structure, and the LORD searches the heart and tries the reins. Third, that where the plague is in the warp the sentence is fire, and no laundering will avert it — which is why the sinner’s hope has never been improvement. Christ does not scour the old garment; He clothes us in another. Read Lev 13 as the ceremonial shadow it is, and it drives you to the same place Isaiah’s crimson does: not to the washtub, but to the Lamb.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The lengthwise threads of the loom — the frame of the cloth; in Lev 13 the depth into which the plague may run.

expand to see more

Warp — Saxon wearp, from weorpan, to cast or throw upon the beams.

Hebrew shethi, the set thread, from a root meaning to set or place (Lev 13:48).

Always paired in Scripture with woof ('erebh), the thread thrown across it.

Nine occurrences, all within the garment-leprosy law of Lev 13:48-59.

The priest, not the launderer, pronounces upon it: clean or unclean before God.

Usage

"Sin is not a stain on the cloth but a plague in the warp — hence a new garment, not a washing."

"The priest examined the structure, not the surface: God tries the frame of a man, not his appearance."

"Where the plague was in the warp, fire was the sentence — a shadow of the judgment reformation cannot avert."
